sections.summary: The author, an Uzbek‑Kyrgyz citizen, was sentenced in absentia by the Jalalabad City Court to 14 years for alleged separatist acts, without prior notice or legal representation; subsequent appeals to the Regional Court and Supreme Court were rejected.

sections.label: Issue and actual outcome
sections.summary: The author alleged violations of ICCPR arts 14(1), 14(2), 14(3)(d) & (e) and related provisions. The Committee concluded that the communication was admissible and found violations of the fair‑trial guarantees, adopting its Views accordingly.

sections.label: Deciding body's reasoning
sections.summary: The Committee held that trial in absentia, without proper notice and opportunity to defend, breaches article 14(3)(d) & (e); it also determined that the parliamentary resolution prejudicing the presumption of innocence violated article 14(2).

sections.label: General comparison factors and limits
sections.summary: The Committee noted that absentia trials may be permissible only when the accused knowingly waives presence after adequate notice; any public statements presuming guilt or legislative commentary that influences the judiciary exceed permissible limits.

  Trial in absentia
2. According to article 14 (3) (d) of the Covenant, everyone is entitled to be tried in his
presence and to defend himself in person or through legal assistance. On the other hand, as
the present Views point out, criminal proceedings in the absence of the accused may in some
circumstances be permissible in the interest of the proper administration of justice, that is,
when the accused pers on, although informed of the proceedings sufficiently in advance,
declines to exercise their right to be present. However, it is important to note that a trial in
the presence of the accused is the principle, while a trial in absentia is the exception.
